items.title: Ahmedabad set to host first Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship from Oct 23
items.summary:
Ahmedabad will host the inaugural Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship from October 23 to 31, bringing together 13 nations for nine days of the competition.
Organised by the Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI) with the approval of the International Kabaddi Federation (IKF), the championship will feature 23 squads and more than 400 athletes competing in 62 matches.
The championship was formally unveiled at a curtain-raiser event on Wednesday.
The Indian men's team will be captained by Surjeet Singh, while Nidhi Sharma will lead the women's team.
The participating nations are India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Canada, Singapore, Malaysia, Uganda, England, Scotland, and Australia.
The semifinals in both categories will take place on October 30, followed by the finals on October 31.
"It is a proud moment for Indian kabaddi to host the first Commonwealth Championship in Ahmedabad," said AKFI secretary Jitendra Pran Singh Thakur in a statement.

Dawood Ibrahim is in Pakistan: India at UN
items.summary: New York: India on Wednesday (local time) strongly hit out at the UN rapporteurs for bias in a counter-terror report and called for high standards of impartiality.UN rapporteur Ben Saul in his report had described Dawood Ibrahim as the leader of the "India-based" D-Company criminal gang with terrorist ties.Taking umbrage at this, Indian diplomat Raghoo Puri told the UN Assembly, "We express serious concern at the unacceptable situation of the SR releasing reports with factual inaccuracies, while not being held accountable for them. This presents Member States with a fait accompli, which is unfortunate for this organization that is facing challenges of legitimacy."Also read: India urges orderly, time-bound transition for UN mechanism continuing work of tribunals on genocide, war crimesPuri underlined that Dawood was a wanted criminal and was based in Pakistan, a country in which Osama bin Laden had been found and neutralized.#WATCH | New York | While participating in the interactive Dialogue with Special Rapporteur, First Secretary Raghoo Puri says, "...My delegation has been pointing out in other forums as well our serious concern about the unacceptable situation of the SR (Special Rapporteur) releasing reports with factual inaccuracies while not being held accountable for them. This presents member states with a fait accompli, which is unfortunate for this organization that is facing challenges of legitimacy... The report mentions that in 2003, the Security Council listed the leader of one criminal group, D-Company, for association with Al-Qaeda... This organization and its listed leader, Dawood Ibrahim, have been wanted in India for terror attacks since 1993. This is clearly written in the narrative summary of reasons for listing under the 1267 sanctions regime. Not mentioning this fact is regrettable, and such incompetence on the part of special mandate holders does this organization tremendous harm... To date, he remains a wanted criminal in my country and, as per the UN's listing entry, resides in the same country where Osama bin Laden was found and neutralized... We also note the clear bias in different parts of the report and also note with concern certain media allegations against this important office. We would urge that the highest standards of probity and impartiality be maintained..."He adds, "It seems to have become fashionable for sponsors of terror to use human rights and the framework of counter-terrorism to justify their misdeeds... Regarding the statement just made by the delegate of Pakistan, everyone in this room knows that what has been mentioned against my country, including about the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, is pure propaganda made for very narrow political gains. These have been made by the actual rulers of Pakistan, which is its military... J&K and Ladakh are an inalienable part of India and have been so and will always remain. I would not like to dignify the statement by the Pakistani delegate with any further comment."(Source: X/Permanent Mission of India to the United Nations, New York)— ANI (@ANI) October 22, 2026"The report mentions that in 2003, the Security Council listed the leader of one criminal group, D-Company, for association with Al-Qaeda. Read in isolation, this line paints a very different picture from the actual reality. This organization and its listed leader, Dawood Ibrahim, has been wanted in India for terror attacks since 1993. This is clearly written in the narrative summary of reasons of listing under the 1267 sanctions regime. Not mentioning this fact is regrettable, and such incompetent- incompetence on part of special mandate holders does this organization tremendous harm. Let me correct it for the record. This individual fled India much before the 2003 listing, and it was during this period, from outside our country, that he was listed for being associated with Al-Qaeda and with Osama bin Laden. To date, he remains a wanted criminal in my country, and as per the UN's listing entry, resides in the same country where Osama bin Laden was found and neutralized," the Indian diplomat said.India also hit out at the bias in the report saying that human right framework can't judge perpetrators of terror."It seems to have become fashionable for sponsors of terror to use human rights and the framework of counterterrorism to justify their misdeeds. Human rights framework cannot be the refuge of the perpetrators of terror and those who propagate radicalization and extremism. Terrorism can never be justified," he said.Puri also hit out at a remark made by the Pakistdelegation, reaffirming that Jammu and Kashmir were integral parts of India."Regarding the statement just made by the delegate of Pakistan, everyone in this room knows that what has been mentioned against my country, including about the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, is pure propaganda made for very narrow political gains. And these have been on account of the actual rulers of Pakistan, which is its military. I would like to reiterate for the record that Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are an inalienable part of India, and have been so, and will always remain. I would not like to dignify the statement of- by the Pakistani delegate with any further comment," he said.On Tuesday, India had asserted that human rights should not be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective country targeting, while calling for accountability, transparency and cooperation to address enforced disappearances at the United Nations General Assembly's Third Committee.Delivering India's statement on the agenda item concerning the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances, Ministry of External Affairs Deputy Secretary Barkha Tamrakar highlighted the constitutional and institutional safeguards available in India to address allegations of human rights violations.

items.summary: Aichi-Nagoya: India's Suvarna Raj won the gold medal in the women's discus throw F54 event at the Asian Para Games 2026 with a best effort of 15.66 metres, securing the country's first gold medal of the day on Thursday.Competing in a six-athlete field, Suvarna delivered a consistent performance, recording four throws beyond the 15-metre mark across her six attempts.Her gold-medal-winning effort came in her fifth attempt, helping her finish at the top of the podium and add another gold to India's medal tally at the continental para-sporting event.Iran's Shahla Hadidi secured the silver medal with a best throw of 15.45 metres, while Vietnam's Nguyen Thi Ngoc Thuy claimed bronze with an effort of 14.65 metres.Suvarna's victory marked a strong start to the day for the Indian contingent as the country's athletes continued their campaign at the Asian Para Games. Her medal marked India's 15th gold at the Games.Meanwhile, Indian para-shuttlers Manisha Ramadass and Pramod Bhagat settled for the bronze medal in the mixed doubles SL3-SU5 event after losing their semifinal against Indonesia's Oktila LeRatri and Hikmat Ramdani.The Indian pair went down 21-16, 13-21, 17-21 in a three-game contest, conceding the match after winning the opening game.Ratri and Ramdani will now face India's Thulasimathi Murugesan and Nitesh Kumar in the final, setting up an opportunity for India to secure the gold medal in the event.Earlier today, Indian para-archer Swati Chaudhary won the silver medal in the women's W1 individual archery event after losing to China's Mengkan Cen 4-6.Swati had a chance to win India's first gold medal in archery at the ongoing edition, taking a 4-2 lead after three ends. However, Cen staged a comeback to win the final 6-4, leaving the Indian archer with the silver medal.With the three medals won so far in the day, India's medal tally now stands at 65 medals with 15 gold medals, 22 silver medals and 28 bronze medals.

India's Ambassador to the United States Vinay Mohan Kwatra, USPS Senior Vice President Shibani Gambhir and Bhutada unveiled the stamp at a function at the Indian embassy here on Wednesday evening.
The USPS described rangoli as a vibrant floor pattern traditionally made from materials, such as coloured rice powder, chalk and flower petals, and believed to bring good luck.
Bhutada is a native of India and a longtime resident of the Houston area. He has practised the ancient folk art of rangoli for nearly 30 years.
The stamp was designed by Jennifer Arnold, and William J Gicker was the art director.

This year, momentum continued even through Shradh, a period considered inauspicious.Also Read: Navratri shoppers splurge on clothes, appliances as gadgets get pricier"The dip is largely optical: last year Navratri ran 11 days against ten and coincided with the GST 2.0 rollout," said FADA president Sai Giridhar.Maruti Suzuki India, the largest carmaker, said Navratri deliveries were about 98% of last year, and it could have sold more with better supply. "Non-availability of vehicles is an issue. If I had more, we would have sold more. Every dealer is asking for more," said Partho Banerjee, senior executive officer-sales and marketing at Maruti. The company gets 12,000-12,500 bookings daily but can supply only 8,000-8,500. Pending bookings rose to 2.7 lakh after Dussehra from about 2 lakh at the start of October.Also Read: Carmakers gear up with multi-powertrain models as Indian buyers shift beyond petrol, dieselJATO Dynamics data shows registrations of petrol, diesel and CNG cars at the top makers fell 5.2% to 1.69 lakh units. Maruti registered 74,387 cars, up 0.1%. Tata Motors fell 16.4% to 24,843 units, Hyundai 2.7% to 19,706 and Kia 9.3% to 9,731, while Mahindra & Mahindra rose 6.6% to 20,681. It said electric car registrations also fell 5.1% to 11,478 units.Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles said demand remained strong. "The response during Navratri has been particularly encouraging, with over 50,000 vehicles delivered during this festive period, including more than 10,000 on Dussehra alone," said Amit Kamat, chief commercial officer, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles.Hyundai Motor India said registrations during Shradh and Navratri grew 30% to nearly 41,000 units. "Considering the pace of bookings, we expect momentum to continue through Dhanteras and Diwali," said chief executive officer Tarun Garg.Dealers said the real picture will emerge in a few days. "We will get to know the real picture after a few days as Vahan portal captures registration with a lag," said a dealer principal.

items.title: How the Mecca defense agreement works
items.summary: Ankara: Turkey's government has asked parliament to ratify a mutual defense agreement it signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, bringing the country closer to bolstering Saudi defenses as it faces attacks from Iran-backed Houthi rebels.Mirroring NATO's Article 5, the so-called Mecca Joint Defense Agreement commits the sides to view an armed attack against one as an attack on all three.While Turkey says that it's considering sending military support to Saudi Arabia, officials have cautioned that the pact is defensive in nature and that no Turkish troops will be deployed to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis.Turkish and Pakistani officials have also insisted that the pact isn't against Iran or any other country, but haven't said how they would react if attacked by Iran.Regional countries take responsibility for their securityThe agreement was signed in the Saudi holy city of Mecca in August by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif with the aim of increasing cooperation and deterrence among the three regional heavyweights at a time of increased uncertainty amid the Iran war.It brings together oil-rich Saudi Arabia and nuclear power Pakistan as well as Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a rapidly growing defense industry. It enables the three to take greater charge for their own security at a time of reduced U.S. involvement.For Pakistan, the Mecca Agreement builds on existing military ties with Riyadh. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a separate mutual defense agreement in September 2025.Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has repeatedly said that the Mecca agreement doesn't replace existing agreements and is open to other countries willing to uphold its principles and resolve differences peacefully.Nature of assistance planned is still unknownDuring an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month, the three countries agreed to immediately implement what they said were their collective defense commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia. They didn't elaborate.Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said that Turkey and Pakistan were assessing possible air defense, electronic warfare and technical assistance for Saudi Arabia."What type of assistance can be provided, especially in areas such as air defense and electronic warfare, what technical support can be offered? Work on these issues is ongoing," he said."Turkey will not be sending troops into another country's territory to carry out an attack. It is a defense agreement," Fidan said, addressing concerns raised by opposition parties that Turkey would be drawn into the conflict in Yemen.Authorities in Pakistan have declined to disclose deployment details, citing operational confidentiality. Officials say, however, that Pakistan's role would be strictly defensive. The Pakistani Information Ministry recently dismissed as "speculative" news reports that said Pakistan had already deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia.Comment from Saudi Arabia on the pact since the Houthi attacks has been limited. In a post on X following a visit by Pakistan's army chief, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman said: "We affirmed our commitment to continuing joint efforts to confront these attacks in accordance with the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense."10-year commitment to the pactLittle was known about the content of the pact until Turkey's government submitted it to parliament for approval on Tuesday.The 16-article agreement, published by Turkish state broadcaster TRT on its website, states that the countries would defend each other militarily in case of external aggression in line with the U.N. Charter's right of self-defense.The agreement also paves the way for military cooperation, including joint training programs, exercises and personnel exchanges. It allows cooperation in the defense industry, including joint weapons production and technology transfers as well as intelligence sharing.A surprise clause states that the parties wouldn't be able to withdraw from the pact for 10 years, after which they would need to provide a three-month notice to leave.A parliamentary committee is expected to review the agreement in the coming days before it reaches the Turkish parliament's general assembly for ratification. Separately, Turkey's parliament would have to authorize any deployment of Turkish military personnel.Pakistan's potential contributionsPakistan hasn't sought parliamentary endorsement of the Mecca agreement, but officials say the government and other national institutions support it. They say Islamabad would provide whatever military assistance Saudi Arabia needs to defend the kingdom and Islam's holiest sites.Pakistan's military has more than two decades of experience fighting militant groups, which analysts say could help it bolster Saudi defenses.The agreement builds on decades of Pakistani military service in Saudi Arabia. An unspecified number of Pakistani troops have been stationed in Saudi Arabia since the early 1980s to train and advise Saudi forces.Pact to be led by retired Pakistani generalEven before the ratification process has been completed, the three countries established and convened a meeting of the so-called Strategic Political and Defense Committee composed of the foreign ministers, defense ministers and chiefs of staff.The committee is expected to meet twice a year.The pact's secretariat will be based in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general. He will serve a three-year term.

items.title: Essar Ports wins ₹2,276 crore Tuna Tekra terminal project at Kandla
items.summary:
Essar Ports has secured a letter of award from Deendayal Port Authority to develop an 18.33-million-tonne-a-year multipurpose cargo terminal at Tuna Tekra in Gujarat's Kandla port, marking a renewed push by the group to expand its ports business.
The project carries an estimated cost of Rs 2,276.06 crore, including an investment of Rs 1,552.57 crore by Essar Ports and Rs 723.49 crore by the port authority, the company said in a statement.
The terminal will be developed under a 30-year build-operate-transfer concession through the public-private partnership route, with Essar emerging as the highest bidder in a global competitive bidding process.
The project will add capacity for handling dry and other multipurpose cargo on India's western coast, as the country seeks to expand port infrastructure to accommodate growing trade and improve logistics efficiency, it said.
The proposed facility will have four berths, each measuring 300 metres, providing a total berth length of 1,200 metres

items.title: India must make growth employment-intensive, not just fast: Ex-RBI chief
items.summary:
Sustaining economic growth of 7 per cent or more will require stronger private investment, labour-intensive manufacturing, better human capital and deeper integration into global value chains, former RBI Governor D Subbarao has said.
Subbarao also said that the challenge is not merely to grow fast, but to make growth productive, employment-intensive and resilient.
"India's 7.8 per cent growth in the first quarter suggests that the economy is more resilient than many expected...I am optimistic about India's medium-term prospects, but not complacent," he told PTI.
Recently, the World Bank raised India's GDP growth forecast for the current fiscal year to 7.1 per cent, up 0.5 percentage points from its April projections, supported by robust domestic demand and strong exports, despite global headwinds.
"Sustaining growth of 7 per cent or more will require stronger private investment, labour-intensive manufacturing, better human capital and deeper integration into global value chains..

items.title: DDA may launch tethered hot air balloon rides in Delhi from November 14
items.summary:
The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) may start its tethered hot air balloon rides from November 14, officials said on Wednesday.
The rides were launched last November from Baanseera park in Sarai Kale Khan area.
"We plan to start the rides from November 14 for the public, the weather is ideal for the launch of the rides and it will be in the same format like last year," a private organiser said.
Ticket prices are likely to be less than last year to attract more customers, he added.
The organisers set the ticket price at around Rs 2,300 per person last time.
DDA, last year, finalised the Yamuna Sports Complex, the Commonwealth Games sports complexes, and Asita and Baansera, two sites along the Yamuna Bank, for balloon rides.
Expansion plans, beyond Baanseera, are on hold.
A trip normally lasts between 7 and 12 minutes, with four people in the balloon.

items.title: Stephen Hubbard’s long road to release
items.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday, at the start of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff. The 74-year-old retired teacher had been serving a prison sentence in Russia after a court convicted him of being a mercenary in Ukraine.Hubbard's case drew attention because of his age, the circumstances surrounding his capture and conflicting accounts of his alleged involvement in the war.Who is Stephen Hubbard?Hubbard grew up in Big Rapids, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force and National Guard, according to military records cited by *The New York Times*.He later earned a master's degree in English and spent 25 years in Japan teaching the language. He subsequently moved to Cyprus before settling in Izyum, a city in eastern Ukraine, in 2014 with a Ukrainian partner, his sister Patricia Hubbard Fox told Reuters.Fox said in 2024 that her brother lived on a pension of around $300 a month and had limited contact with local residents. The siblings last spoke in September 2021.How was Hubbard captured?Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and captured Izyum two months later. Ukrainian forces recaptured the city in September that year, but Hubbard was already in Russian custody.Russian state media reported that he had been detained in April 2022 and alleged that he was manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Reuters could not independently establish the circumstances of his capture.Fox said she recognised her brother in a YouTube video showing a man being questioned about his views on Putin and the war. A separate video appeared to show the man with his hands bound and being struck with a sandal. Reuters could not verify when or where the footage was recorded.Why was he imprisoned in Russia?In October 2024, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary following a closed trial and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison.Prosecutors alleged that he had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and been promised a monthly payment of $1,000. Russian state media reported that he had pleaded guilty.His sister questioned that account, saying Hubbard held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms at his age.Martin De Luca, Hubbard's US-based lawyer, told Reuters in June 2025 that his client denied the allegations. According to De Luca, Hubbard said he had never belonged to a combat or military unit and that Russian soldiers had taken him from his home.What happened during his detention?The US State Department designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained in January 2025, allowing Washington to pursue efforts to secure his release. The department said Russia had denied US officials consular access to him.The New York Times reported in February 2025 that Hubbard had been transferred between at least five Russian detention centres before his trial.His legal team learnt only in April 2025 that he was being held at a facility in the Mordovia region, east of Moscow, De Luca said.Putin's announcement on Wednesday marks a significant development in Hubbard's case. Further details of the circumstances of his release were not immediately available in the information provided.

The NDMC will distinguish structural additions and alterations from routine maintenance and non-structural renovation, providing clarity on which works are exempt and which require prior approval, Dwivedi said.
He said the civic body would also launch an awareness campaign to ensure building users are not inconvenienced or confused by compliance requirements.

Poll interference is hard. Fooling voters is easy
items.summary: You’ve likely heard the ominous what-if scenarios about election disruptions in November: immigration agents or federal troops roaming polling places, federal officials seizing ballots and voting machines, and President Donald Trump issuing an executive order postponing or cancelling the election. Courts and legal experts have given solid reasons that each one of those potential election disruptions is unlikely. But the threats have served their purpose: People are harbouring doubts.The federal government doesn’t have to interfere with the mechanics of the voting process to disrupt the election. The easiest way for bad actors to interfere in the midterm elections right now is to let fear and distrust mess with our minds. By intimidating people into thinking they’ll face harassment at the polls or casting doubt on the integrity of the process, the administration is planting the seeds that the results can’t be trusted.I recently spoke with a naturalized US citizen from Venezuela who lives in Miami. She’s a young professional, married with kids, and until recently had been an active member of her local political party. She’s a reliable voter, but she told me she won’t be voting in person this year. The ICE raids that have terrorized her community have left her and her neighbors isolated and afraid.“I don’t want to go and vote in person, because I am terrified that they’re going to bring out the National Guard,” she told me. “You know, I have PTSD.”This is where Trump has brought us: US citizens fear risking their safety to exercise their constitutional right to vote.For the last 21 months, the federal government has mounted an unprecedented attack on state sovereignty over elections. Trump signed two executive orders that seek to radically dictate state election policy. The Department of Justice sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to gain access to sensitive voter data. The White House seized Georgia’s ballots from the 2020 election. And Trump tried to rehash his election conspiracy theories in a prime-time speech earlier this year.Judges from county courthouses to the US Supreme Court have rebuffed much of it. But the effort has undercut voter confidence. A University of Georgia survey of more than 11,000 voters found only 58% of Republicans, 63% of Democrats, and 49% of Independents trusted that votes would be counted accurately nationwide. And a recent poll from AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that only 34% of US adults trust government certifications of election results “a great deal” or “quite a bit,” down from 40% in 2024.Sometimes all it takes is a headline to sow doubt. That’s what happened in 2016 when Russian hackers got access to the Illinois state voter registration database. The hackers went unnoticed for weeks and only when they started accessing thousands of records per second did Illinois election officials shut the system down.“Russia wanted to be noticed,” said David Becker, who runs the non-partisan election watchdog site The Center for Election Innovation and Research. “They wanted the American people to think that our foreign adversaries had … the ability to change our elections.” Since then, US adversaries, particularly Russia, Iran and China, have focused on manipulating social media to make voters, particularly supporters of losing candidates, believe that their elections were stolen.Fortunately, millions of voters haven’t been intimidated by these global or domestic scare tactics. Records indicate that two weeks into early voting, an unprecedented number of votes have already been cast across the country, in many states exceeding records broken in 2018, 2022 and 2024.And in unprecedented fashion, state elections officials have locked arms in a bipartisan effort to resist any attempt by the administration to interfere.State officials are taking a traditional “all hazards approach,” said Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon, who leads the National Association of Secretaries of State. They’re prepared to handle election disruptions involving everything from natural disasters and bomb threats to power outages. This year, he told me, they’ve added “federal interference.”States have amassed teams of lawyers who are prepared to act quickly in the unlikely event that federal troops do show up, said Becker. They are also prepared to get before a judge if federal officials attempt to seize election equipment and get a ruling “before the chain of custody is irrevocably damaged,” he explained.But as a reminder, it’s a crime for anyone to order federal troops to a polling place — a violation punishable by up to five years in prison, a fine and disqualification from public office. Federal laws bar Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from the polls. And it’s logistically impossible for Trump to cancel an election because thousands of officials across the country control elections, not the White House.The internet is an inviting host for allowing the mischief to continue in the weeks ahead. Let’s keep our wits about us. Thank the hard-working elections officials who keep the system sound, and don’t be duped.

He also cited birth tourism as an example, saying it involved other countries rather than India."Frankly, we have seen many of these programmes being abused. Again, it is not unique to Indians or India," he said. "So we are trying to fix 20 years of neglect of an immigration system… and that is not targeted towards India," Rubio added.Why India feels the impactRubio acknowledged that changes to the US visa system can have a significant impact on Indians because of the large number of applicants from the country in some visa categories."Now, obviously, because of the developments, because of the ties between our countries, because of how developed your economy is, there are certain categories of visas that see a large number of Indians applying for," he said.The US, he said, still wants foreign students, workers, visitors and investors, but wants immigration to take place under laws that are followed."We want people to visit the United States. We want people to study in the United States. There are certain people that we want, that want to come work for a time in the United States. We want people to invest in the United States, and we are always going to have people immigrate to the United States," Rubio said."But we want it done through a system of laws that are complied with," he added.'Biggest threat to legal immigration is illegal immigration'Rubio also sought to draw a distinction between legal immigration and illegal immigration, arguing that large-scale unauthorised migration could undermine legal pathways."The biggest threat to legal immigration is illegal immigration. The biggest threat to legal immigration is mass migration, which again is not an Indian phenomenon (but) more unique to other parts of the world," he said.Rubio acknowledged that US policy changes could appear to be directed at India because of their effect on Indian applicants, but rejected that interpretation."And while I know that from your perspective here in India, it may seem targeted at India, (but) it’s not," he said."There is virtually no country on Earth that I visit where I don’t get a complaint about some visa or process, because we are fixing it globally."Rubio said the administration believed the changes would eventually make US immigration programmes more sustainable."Once it’s fixed, it will be far more sustainable. I actually think it will be better for the people using those programmes, and right and good for the United States," he said.

items.title: Dr Reddy's receives DCGI approval for esophageal cancer drug Zytorvi
items.summary:
Dr Reddy's Laboratories on Wednesday said it has received approval from the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) for Zytorvi (toripalimab), through which it aims to expand access to first-line immunotherapy for patients with advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) in India.
The drug has been approved in combination with cisplatin and paclitaxel for the first-line treatment of adult patients with unresectable advanced, recurrent, or metastatic ESCC, the pharma company said in a release.
This marks Zytorvi's second approved indication in the country, expanding beyond nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
ESCC accounts for approximately 80 per cent of all esophageal cancer cases in India, the company said.
Zytorvi contains toripalimab, a monoclonal antibody that binds to PD-1 and blocks its interaction with PD-L1 and PD-L2, thereby supporting T-cell activity against cancer cells.

items.title: France has a proud tradition of protesting
items.summary: PARIS - No nation does mass protests quite like France.When the French fight high fuel taxes, they don yellow vests and march. When angry farmers want better pay, hundreds of them drive tractors down the Champs-Elysees. And when museum workers want better tourist management, they strike and shut down the Louvre.Passionate public protest is as French as "La Marseillaise," the 1792 anthem that enshrines the collective duty to fight tyranny in the country's national identity. But this month, the most violent demonstrations in years - and tough policing - have raised concern about riots overshadowing hundreds of thousands of peaceful demonstrators marching against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.Also read: France unrest leaves global brands with a burning problemOn Saturday alone, at least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings, looted stores and engulfed a historic city hall in flames. More protests could be in store."How can French people do this to France?" outgoing President Emmanuel Macron asked on Sunday. Nothing justifies the destruction, he added. "We all feel anger and shame."But any student of French history would know that the nation's proud, loud and colorful protest culture has sometimes turned violent - starting with the beheadings of King Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette during the revolution that overthrew the monarchy in 1789.A protest culture is bornHistorians say the revolution was where the modern-day French tradition of civic engagement as a duty was born. The idea is that voting is not the only way to drive change; demonstration is considered a bedrock value, a way to make elites hear the populace and to defend freedoms. The moment a child becomes an activist is seen as a generations-old rite of passage. The right to protest is even constitutionally protected."It's a way to build collective identity and political community," said Magali Della Sudda, research director in political science at the French National Center for Scientific Research in Bordeaux.France's post-revolution history is not a solid story of protests and reforms, but of cycles of popular uprisings, repression, mobilization and political concessions. The tradition has turned tragic; In 1871, government troops cracked down on the new "Paris Commune," or municipal government, reportedly killing thousands.In some ways, collective action won - as in 1968, when student demonstrations and a general strike forced the government to grant concessions like an increase in the minimum wage.In more recent history, the "yellow vests" - "gilets jaunes" in French - demonstrated against a proposed fuel tax increase, and that broadened into protests over other issues like living costs and inequality. Some demonstrations in 2018 and 2019 featured burning cars, looting and confrontations with police. It's not uncommon for French violence on the fringes to mar otherwise peaceful marches.Likewise, the student protests over the weekend expanded from education to other grievances - and featured dramatic scenes of looting and clashes with police. It's not clear how many of those who were ransacking shops had turned out to join the day's protest, which drew tens of thousands, or were mere opportunists. Authorities have responded with nightly curfews; there were calls for more protests later in the week.Also read: With France embroiled in protest, a look at the nation's economic standing by the numbersPolice violence blamed for mistrustSome of the forces driving protests for the last month owe to more recent French tradition, according to political scientist Fabien Jobard, who has studied the history of protest and policing.Since the 1990s, the country has seen recurring waves of what the French call "violences urbaines" and Americans would call riots, Jobard said. They are often sparked by police violence: nationwide unrest erupted in 2005 after two teenagers died while fleeing police, and again in 2023 after an officer fatally shot a 17-year-old during a traffic stop outside Paris."For young people from the suburbs, the riot is one of the traditional forms of collective expression," he said.Government critics and human rights campaigners have alleged that police tactics in the last month have been unnecessarily violent. Much of the criticism focuses on rubber-bullet launchers, known in France as LBDs, and stun grenades, which critics blame for serious injuries to protesters.And Della Sudda noted that the nearly 8,000 arrests in the weeks leading up to Oct. 17 dwarf the few dozen detained during a 1998 protest of 500,000 students against teacher shortages and dilapidated schools.The feeling of not being heard also is part of it, she says. Rather than listen to protesters and negotiate, Della Sudda noted for example, the government tried to appease "yellow vest" grievances through a digital platform, which translates to "the great national debate." Anti-government protesters panned Macron's plan."As a result," Della Sudda wrote, "mistrust is growing."

Delhi Police on Tuesday transferred another case registered against Cockroach Janta Party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka to the Crime Branch, sources said.
The Crime Branch will now investigate two cases against the CJP leaders. The other case linked to Das and Ranka allegedly entering the Jantar Mantar area was transferred to the Crime Branch on Monday.
According to Delhi Police, on October 13, Das, Ranka, Ajinkya Shinde and 11 other members of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) reached Jantar Mantar, which has been denotified as a designated protest site, by trespassing through private premises.
Police personnel deployed at the spot intervened and tried to stop them. All 14 people were detained and two FIRs were registered.
Das and Ranka were sent to five-day judicial custody on October 14 by a Special Executive Magistrate for breaching peace bonds. Their judicial custody was extended by two days on Monday.

items.title: Philanthropy’s biggest failure is its fear of failure
As slow as an India-US trade deal
items.summary: There are forces who have probably been assigned the task of ensuring that Marco Rubio doesn't overhear this during the next few days he's here in India. But India is a big and loud place, and this corner column only mirrors it. So, consider our duty to put on record a new idiomatic phrase in English that has gained traction over the last few months: 'As slow as an India-US trade deal'.Those familiar with formulations such as 'watching paint dry' and 'waiting for Godot' may already know what we're talking about. Except, this latest idiom describes an activity that is simultaneously happening, not happening, and about to happen.Its most remarkable feature is its elasticity. A delayed flight is merely late. A delayed marriage may be called off. But something proceeding 'as slow as an India-US trade deal' enjoys permanent forward momentum without the inconvenience of arriving.Whenever an official announces that negotiations are 'almost complete', seasoned observers understand that it's nudge-nudge, wink-wink for another postponement. 'We are very close' means further away than previously feared. 'Final stages' suggests the beginning of another round. 'Constructive discussions' indicates that nobody has thrown a chair. Trade negotiators on both sides of the Indo-Pacific water table have finally produced something of lasting value: a phrase.

items.title: France: Curfews bring calm to Paris
items.summary: PARIS: Paris returned to calm on Tuesday after its first quiet night since a weekend marred by France's most destructive rioting in years, as authorities imposed curfews in several cities in an effort to prevent another round of rioting and looting.At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings and engulfed a historic city hall in flames, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities.Also Read: Paris police issue overnight curfew in 2 areas of French capital to try to prevent further disorderIn the capital, a curfew ran from 11 p.m. on Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday, and a police helicopter circled over Place de la Republique overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the order was being respected.Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, a reference to the " yellow vest " protests over fuel prices that began in 2018 and shook the first term of President Emmanuel Macron.Workers then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument."The targeted curfews helped keep last night calm," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X on Tuesday, adding that new curfews would be imposed that night "wherever the situation requires," decided locally by prefects, the state's representatives in each region, together with mayors.Speaking in Lille, northern France, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,500 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing.In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the Oct. 17 protests, the city prosecutor's office said in a statement.Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. "People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of," he said, arguing that the French justice system will be "extremely firm."In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and imprisoned immediately for looting a video game store in the city's old town.The National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament, is launching an inquiry into the Oct. 17 violence and the authorities' policing strategy, its speaker, Yael Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected "by the end of the year."
